The patient presents with acute-onset sharp lower back pain radiating along the lateral leg to the foot — a classic dermatomal distribution consistent with L5 or S1 radiculopathy. The lateral leg and foot radiation strongly favors L5 (which innervates the dorsum of the foot and great toe) or possibly the proximal S1 (lateral heel/ankle), though S1 more typically radiates posteriorly. - Acute onset of sharp lower back pain during gym exercise (mechanical trigger consistent with disc herniation).  
- Pain radiates along the lateral leg to the foot (classic L5 dermatomal pattern: L4–L5 disc compresses L5 root → lateral thigh, lateral calf, dorsum of foot, great toe).  
- No bowel or bladder dysfunction (argues against cauda equina, supports isolated single-root involvement).  
- No subjective numbness/tingling in foot dorsum, lateral ankle, or sole (suggests sensory irritation may be subclinical or early; absence doesn’t negate radiculopathy — pain can precede sensory symptoms).

- Straight leg raise (SLR) and crossed SLR results not obtained — key bedside tests for radicular irritation.  
- MRI findings pending — definitive confirmation of disc herniation location, size, and neural compression required.  
- No assessment of gait, stance, or provocative maneuvers (e.g., Valsalva, cough) to elicit radicular pain.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
L5 radiculopathy

[THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with acute-onset sharp lower back pain radiating along the lateral leg to the foot — a classic dermatomal distribution consistent with L5 or S1 radiculopathy. The lateral leg and foot radiation strongly favors L5 (which innervates the dorsum of the foot and great toe) or possibly the proximal S1 (lateral heel/ankle), though S1 more typically radiates posteriorly. Crucially, the *absence* of reported numbness/tingling in the foot (dorsum, lateral ankle, sole) or groin/buttock, and no bowel/bladder dysfunction, effectively rules out cauda equina syndrome and makes severe nerve root compromise less likely — but does not exclude acute radicular irritation from a new disc herniation. The provoking event (gym exercise) is typical for mechanical disc injury. While formal neurological testing (e.g., strength for great toe extension, SLR) is pending, the *pattern* of radicular pain — especially its lateral leg-to-foot trajectory — is highly specific for L5 radiculopathy. L4 radiculopathy would more commonly refer to the anterior thigh/knee; S1 to the posterior calf/heel. MRI is pending, but the clinical picture is already strongly suggestive. Among disc-related radiculopathies, L5 is the most common level affected (especially at L4–L5), and the symptom distribution aligns best with L5.
